journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Early-Career Music Teachers: Collegiate Experiences, Job Satisfaction, and Predictors of Retention
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine music education alumni perceptions of their undergraduate degree experiences, career attainment, career satisfaction, and the extent to which various educational, career, and/or demographic variables increased the likelihood of them remaining in the teaching profession. Data for this study were gleaned from the Strategic National Arts Alumni Project’s (SNAAP) 2022 survey of nearly 60,000 arts alumni in North America. Early-career music teacher respondents were mostly pleased with their experiences in their undergraduate degree programs, and subsequent job satisfaction was strikingly similar regardless of whether respondents had stayed in or departed the teaching profession. Increased satisfaction with their collegiate education was associated with a 111% increase in the likelihood of them staying in the music teaching profession, and increased feelings of societal contribution were associated with a 256% increase in the likelihood of them staying. Numerous implications suggest ways stakeholders can leverage these data to support teacher satisfaction and retention.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Supporting Early-Career Music Teachers: An Analysis of State Conference Programming
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine sessions offered at state music educator associations’ (MEAs) annual conferences designed to support early-career music teachers (ECMTs). We used qualitative content analysis to examine MEA conference programs ( N = 47) held between August 2023 and August 2024. We categorized conference sessions aimed at ECMTs ( N = 255) according to target audience, mode of delivery, topic, and content. Most sessions followed a clinic format, with the target audience closely divided between preservice teachers and early-career teachers. Four themes emerged in the analysis of session content: (a) unfocused content, (b) first-year teaching, (c) job search, and (d) mentoring. Recommendations for practitioners curating and presenting professional development sessions include focusing on research-based, specific topics; using active and collaborative presentation styles; and implementing strategies for effective mentorship programs.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Music Education, Openness to Experience, and Neuroticism: Are We Making Students Happier?
abstract: The general expectation from music education is that it contributes to the development of positive qualities, such as creativity in individuals, as well as increasing their happiness and well-being. In this study, the extent to which this expectation is met was tested by measuring the neuroticism and openness to experience personality traits of music students. Participants ( N = 466) completed a demographic questionnaire and the Big Five Personality Inventory. We found that music students scored significantly higher on both traits compared with those who did not receive music education. These findings indicate that music education may has a positive effect on the openness to experience trait of music students, especially in females. However, no reducing effect on the neuroticism level was detected. The data obtained show that adopting an educational approach that takes into account the psychological needs of students is necessary to achieve the fundamental goals of music education.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Supporting Autistic Students in Music Education: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Education for autistic students is complex and highly individualized, with most autistic students attending mainstream schools. However, mainstream schools are often not equipped to sufficiently support autistic students, contributing to poorer academic and social outcomes. Music education is a common component of mainstream education worldwide, but research has largely focused on music as an intervention or therapy for autism. Subsequently, this systematic review explores how music classrooms can better support autistic students from a neurodiversity-affirming perspective. Analysis of 21 texts yielded eight key recommendations: using technology, using visual aids, selecting repertoire, adapting instruction, implementing routine and repetition, facilitating peer interaction, utilizing team-based approaches, and fostering inclusive environments. Findings support a holistic approach to music education for autistic students and provide practical recommendations for teacher practice, in alignment with international inclusion guidelines.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Culturally Oriented Asset-Based Pedagogies in Music Education
abstract: The terms culturally relevant and culturally responsive have been part of educational discourse for decades, with culturally sustaining pedagogy emerging more recently. Gloria Ladson-Billings introduced culturally relevant pedagogy in the early 1990s, and subsequent scholars—including Geneva Gay and Django Paris—have extended this work. At the same time, demographic shifts in U.S. public schools show that student populations are now predominantly non-White, whereas the teaching workforce remains largely White. These changes heighten the need for music educators, whose classrooms are deeply embedded in cultural expression, to engage effectively with students whose cultural identities differ from their own. Despite widespread use of these frameworks, misunderstandings regarding their purpose and implementation persist, particularly in applied disciplines, such as music education. This literature review examines culturally relevant, culturally responsive, and culturally sustaining pedagogies, clarifies common misconceptions, and emphasizes moving beyond deficit thinking to support equitable and meaningful music education practice.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Guitar in Music Education: A Review of the Literature
abstract: Guitar is a highly visible instrument in contemporary musical life, yet its role in school music programs has historically been inconsistent and contested. This review of literature synthesizes research on guitar in music education (1,353 sources), examining pedagogical approaches, curriculum and program design, teacher preparation, student outcomes, and issues of access, creativity, and cultural relevance. Sources include theses, dissertations, peer-reviewed and practitioner journals, books, and edited volumes drawn from music education, ethnomusicology, and related fields, with attention to international and culturally diverse contexts. Across the literature, guitar instruction is shown to align closely with student-centered, collaborative, and culturally-responsive pedagogies, often bridging formal and informal learning through peer learning, improvisation, composition, and popular and global repertoire. Researchers have suggested that guitar-centered programs can expand participation, support equity, and enhance engagement for students underserved by traditional ensemble models. Implications for classroom practice, teacher education, and future research are discussed.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Student Engagement in the School Music Ensemble: A Review of Literature
abstract: This literature review examines structural and environmental factors that may influence student engagement in school music ensembles. Drawing from research in music education, educational psychology, cognitive science, and developmental research, the review synthesizes findings across four dimensions of ensemble settings: director-centered authority and student agency, notation dependence and cognitive load, adolescent development and social risk, and identity formation. This review employs three complementary theoretical frameworks, self-determination theory, flow theory, and sociocultural learning theory, as recurring lenses for analyzing how these structural features may support or constrain engagement. The review argues that engagement is shaped not by any single factor but by the interaction among multiple structural conditions operating simultaneously within rehearsal and performance environments. Implications for practice emerge from four design principles: supporting student agency, designing for internalization, creating emotional safety, and fostering musical identity. Directions for future research are identified.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: The Missing Middle: Preparation, Practice, and Equity in Middle School Choral Education in the United States
abstract: In this narrative literature review, we synthesize research on middle school choral education in the United States from 2000 to 2025. Based on the analysis of over 40 empirical and practitioner pieces, three key themes emerged: (a) developmentally responsive pedagogy for adolescent singers, (b) student engagement and motivation, and (c) equity and inclusion. Findings suggest that the importance of relational trust, cultures of belonging, and differentiated developmentally responsive pedagogy are well-supported in the literature. Findings also suggest that gaps remain in terms of preservice preparation for the middle school context as well as uneven attention to gendered voice change. Further, we argue that there is also an aspiration–application divide between goals of equity and classroom practice. Based on the findings, we argue for a need for both technical and relational aspects within teacher education and that middle school choral music represents a vital yet still underexplored context within music education.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: A Critical Analysis of the Representation of Non-Western Cultural Content in Beginning Band Method Books
abstract: The purpose of this critical content analysis was to examine the representation of non-Western song content in six beginning band method books. We examined the prevalence of non-Western musical content, the accuracy of song titles and attributions, and evidence of cultural appropriation. Our findings indicated that the vast majority (82.9%) of the books’ content was Western music. The book authors attributed most non-Western songs to accurate origins. However, when presenting non-Western songs, the books (a) contained some inaccurate song titles and attributions; (b) regularly omitted names of composers and lyricists; (c) disproportionately decontextualized non-Western songs; (d) provided little information about cultures of origin; and (e) employed some colonial frameworks and racist stereotypes in their presentation. These common publishing practices have substantial consequences for student learning, and music educators should consider the ethical and pedagogical need to supplement method books to address their limitations and problematic content.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Comparing Interleaved and Blocked Practices in Secondary School Music Performances
abstract: A well-established principle in cognitive psychology is the interleaving effect, which refers to alternating between different tasks during practice. Although interleaving has been shown to support long-term learning across domains, its application in secondary school music classrooms remains underexplored. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of interleaved and blocked practice schedules on music performance and retention in a general secondary music setting. Intact groups of first-year secondary students ( N = 60) completed an 11-session, 5-week teacher-led intervention while practicing four similar melodic pieces on a recorder. Music performance was assessed at pretest, posttest, and a 4-week follow-up using a performance rubric. Results indicated that both groups improved from pretest to posttest, with no significant between-group differences. At follow-up, however, students in the interleaving group maintained performance levels, whereas those in the blocked condition showed a significant decline. These findings suggest that teacher-directed interleaving may support longer-term retention of music performance skills in secondary general music classrooms.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: The Inhospitality of Inclusion in Music Education
abstract: The purpose of this literature review was to investigate aspects of inclusion in music education that hinder or facilitate the provision of unconditionally hospitable learning environments. I reviewed books and articles within the fields of music education and special education that focused on inclusion. Through Derrida’s theory of hospitality, I identified five barriers to effective inclusion: (a) lack of access to inclusion, (b) attitudes and perceptions, (c) inadequate preparation and training, (d) insufficient access to materials and resources, and (e) confidence. Findings also reflected specific cultural characteristics and strategies as facilitators of effective inclusion. Researchers can explore types of behaviors often resulting in the placement of students in self-contained classrooms and specific ways teachers can adapt the environment and instruction to make inclusion more hospitable.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Teachers’ Use of Pre-Performance Rituals in Music Ensembles: Beliefs and Practices
abstract: This mixed-methods study examined how music educators use pre-performance rituals in ensemble settings and how they perceive their value for students. Twenty-seven Indiana music educators completed a brief online questionnaire, with three participating in follow-up interviews and one rehearsal observation. Most participants (70%) reported using pre-performance rituals with their ensembles, and nearly all (96%) expressed strong beliefs in their benefits. Teachers described four common ritual types: group unity practices, physical and vocal preparation, motivational activities, and mental focus routines. Across these forms, rituals frequently included symbolic elements or traditions passed down within programs. Qualitative findings indicated that teachers used rituals to help students manage performance anxiety, focus attention, build group cohesion, and support student leadership, while balancing long-standing traditions with adaptation to changing student needs. The findings suggest that pre-performance rituals are a common and flexible teaching practice that supports students’ emotional readiness and sense of belonging alongside musical preparation.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Music-Reading Fluency at the Piano for Beginning Children: A Literature Review
abstract: In this literature review, I aim to synthesize empirical and pedagogical research on the multifaceted skills that contribute to music-reading fluency at the piano and to propose a framework to understand how three music-reading approaches (sounds-first, Middle C, and intervallic) may support the development of those skills in beginning piano learners. Findings indicate that the sounds-first approach, often implemented through solfège and early audiation, strongly supports auditory processing and auditory working memory, facilitating symbol-to-sound mapping. The Middle C approach reduces early cognitive and motor demands by anchoring the hands around a reference note, supporting visual decoding and motor automatisms. The intervallic approach challenges learners’ visual-spatial reasoning and motor planning while fostering keyboard flexibility and pattern recognition. A framework summarizing these relationships guides instructional design and identifies gaps for future research, including the potential of longitudinal studies that consider developmental stages.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: A Journey Through Self-Compassion: The Exploration of a Choir-Composer-Conductor Collaboration
abstract: The purpose of this intrinsic case study was to explore a collaboration between two student composers, a collegiate choral ensemble, and a faculty choral conductor in preparation for two new student-composed choral compositions centered on self-compassion. The two student composers each composed a piece of music with texts related to self-compassion. The ensemble rehearsed the pieces for 15 weeks, then performed them at the end of the semester. Data sources included: (a) three interviews with each of the composers, (b) weekly journal entries for each of the composers and the conductor, (c) four focus groups with members of the ensemble, (d) texts from the compositions, and (e) composer conversations with the singers. Using the communities of practice theoretical framework and the self-compassion construct, three themes emerged: increased awareness of self-compassion, excitement in musical shared experience, and community building.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: In-Service Music Educators’ Self-Perceptions of Undergraduate Preparation Across Selected Professional Competencies
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine how in-service K–12 music educators perceived the relationship between selected professional competencies and their own undergraduate preparation. A total of 218 music educators from 46 U.S. states rated their perceptions of the current importance of eight competencies and the extent to which they believed their undergraduate programs had prepared them in those same areas via an online questionnaire. Across all eight competencies, importance ratings were significantly higher than preparation ratings. The largest differences were found in classroom management, student well-being, and inclusion and differentiation, while smaller differences were found in music-specific pedagogy and assessment. Relational and contextual competencies appeared more likely to be perceived as less well addressed in undergraduate preparation. The author suggests consideration of more robust integration of relational domains, such as cultural responsiveness, student well-being, and advocacy, through approaches such as case-based rehearsal scenarios in methods classes and relevant coursework in music teacher preparation programs.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Measuring Wellbeing in a Sixth-Grade Band Program: An Action Research Study
abstract: The purpose of this exploratory, quantitative action research study was to pilot an alternative approach to assessment in one of the author’s sixth-grade bands that included wellbeing rather than meeting standards-based benchmarks alone. Using the Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire (SSWQ), authors surveyed 186 students to measure joy of learning, school connectedness, educational purpose, academic efficacy, and overall wellbeing. Results indicated that students often experienced positive wellbeing across all subscales, though variability suggested areas for improvement, particularly in joy of learning. Findings emphasize the importance of assessing wellbeing alongside musical growth to enhance retention, engagement, and equity in music education. Action steps included implementing early interventions, administering surveys multiple times per year, and expanding wellbeing-informed practices. This study highlights the potential of wellbeing assessment to promote holistic development and advocates for continued cycles of action research to refine strategies for improving student wellbeing in music classrooms.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: The Role of Music in Inquiry-Based Learning: A Literature Review on Reggio Emilia Approaches
abstract: In this literature review, I examined the role of music in inquiry-based learning within early childhood education settings based on the Reggio Emilia approach. Drawing on international studies from the past three decades, the review synthesizes research on early childhood music education in both formal and informal settings. Music emerged as a language of learning—facilitating collaboration, emotional expression, and multimodal exploration. Key findings highlighted the educator’s role in co-constructing musical meaning, the use of documentation to reveal musical thinking, and obstacles to incorporating sound-based inquiry in environments that favor visual approaches. Structural barriers included inadequate teacher training, curricular limitations, and insufficient time for music instruction. I also addressed implications for the field, such as deliberate music integration, advancing interdisciplinary collaboration, and adopting inclusive documentation practices.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Performative Music Education Pathways: Bomba as a Framework for Music Teaching and Learning
abstract: For decades, music education has sought models that move beyond the confines of formal instruction. Performative Music Education (PME) offers a framework for meaningful learning experiences, grounded in philosophical perspectives from diverse fields. PME fosters musical skills, knowledge, and understanding through self-referential processes that emphasize student participation in music creation. This article examines the theoretical foundations of PME while envisioning the integration of Puerto Rican bomba music into formal classrooms through this lens. To explore this, the study analyses the practices of a community music initiative dedicated to bomba. Seen as a cultural territory, bomba provides a space to express ideas, emotions, and affections meaningful to practitioners. Using an instrumental qualitative case study, the research draws on interviews with nine participants and observations. Findings suggest bomba aligns strongly with PME, positioning the framework as a foundation for incorporating traditional music into formal education.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Engaging With On-Demand Digital Media: Music Teachers’ Use and Perceptions
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine how music teachers report using and engaging with on-demand digital media (ODDM) and whether they perceive ODDM content as professional development. K–12 inservice and preservice music teachers ( N = 198) completed a questionnaire that collected information regarding their experiences with ODDM (Facebook, Twitter/X, Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, and podcasts). Results showed that respondents derived usefulness from and followed creators who shared strategies that aligned with classroom teaching needs and whom respondents deemed credible. Respondents discussed classroom applications, such as warm-ups, teaching strategies, concert programming, and performance demonstrations. More than half of the respondents considered their engagement with ODDM to be professional development, but many encountered content they did not believe was credible or aligned with research-based practices. Implications include suggestions for teacher engagement with ODDM along with important considerations for digital media literacy among music teachers.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: A Musical Life-Story of an Imprecise Singer: Belonging, Motivation, and Musical Meaning
abstract: This narrative study traces the musical life of “Frederick,” an imprecise singer, to illuminate how skill, belief, and social context jointly shape music participation choices across the lifespan. Drawing primarily on semi-structured interviews, this musical life-story follows Frederick from childhood to late adulthood, examining how and why he made choices about participating in music. Findings show that participation endured in low-risk, purpose-rich settings where singing functioned as shared practice. This study draws focus to that many singers labeled “out of tune” are better understood as imprecise—musically engaged yet variably accurate—and that early self-concept messages can steer long-term choices in music. Implications translate into concrete applications for music teachers such as protecting student dignity when giving feedback, communicating that accuracy is a learned skill, using “thick” textures to reduce vulnerability, countering gendered messages about music participation, and programming purposeful performances that anchor music in meaning.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Constructivist “Cracks” in Essentialist Vocal Pedagogy: A Review of the Literature on Vocal Gender Perception
abstract: The human voice carries more than sound—it aurally conveys identity. In music education, the voice has often been treated as a sexed instrument, with binary, biological assumptions guiding classification and pedagogy. Using sources across music education, vocal science, and psychology, I explore (a) how listeners perceive gender in speaking and singing, (b) how voices outside gendered norms are perceived externally and internally, and (c) how those perceptions shape choral and vocal pedagogy. Findings reveal that gendered sound is not fixed in anatomy but produced through culture, context, and choice. Voices outside binary norms like transgender and non-binary singers expose both the “cracks” in and the potential harms of essentialist sex-based frameworks. Drawing on recent work in vocal science and gender-affirming voice training, I argue for a constructivist vocal pedagogy that centers singer agency, health, and collaboration—flexing technique and assessment to support authentic, self-congruent singing without sacrificing musical rigor. journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Music Teacher Identity Across the Career Span: A Literature Review
abstract: The purpose of this literature review was to outline and explore the identity construction, developmental pathways, and potential conflicts faced by music teachers at various stages of their careers. Using thematic content analysis, we synthesized research in four areas: the structure and characteristics of music teacher identity, identity conflicts and role negotiation, critical factors influencing music teacher identity formation, and strategies for strengthening and sustaining music teacher identity. The review mapped developmental pathways from preservice through experienced practice and highlighted points where targeted support might be helpful. By clarifying how identities were formed, challenged, and adapted over time, the review offered practical implications for curriculum design, induction, and ongoing professional learning. These insights could help music teachers at different stages clarify and intentionally guide their identity development and professional growth, supporting progress toward expert practice.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: NAfME Eastern Division Elementary Music Teachers’ Perceptions of and Practices Related to Assessment: A Survey Study
abstract: In this study, we documented and compared the assessment perceptions and practices of elementary music educators in NAfME’s Eastern Division. State MEA organizations and NAfME distributed a researcher-designed survey in which respondents ( N = 109) answered Likert-type items and items focused on the use of assessment and feedback strategies. We analyzed results based on participants’ demographics and teaching responsibilities (i.e., choral ensemble, general music, band ensemble, orchestra ensemble, other). Independent of teaching responsibility, these teachers reported overall positive perceptions of assessment’s role in music classrooms. Participants reported using varied assessments and feedback styles in their classrooms; in general, they rely on informal assessment over formal assessment and non-musical grading criteria over musical grading criteria. We recommend replicating and expanding this study throughout the country or as a qualitative or mixed methods inquiry.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Elementary Music Teachers’ Implementation of General Music Approaches and Perceptions of Preparation to Teach Elementary Music
abstract: This descriptive study examined elementary music teachers’ perceptions of their preparation and implementation of general music approaches. Missouri elementary music teachers ( N = 142) participated via email survey. Kodály and Orff Schulwerk were most frequently implemented, accounting for the greatest classroom time allocation, yet most teachers lacked formal credentials in these approaches. Teachers felt most prepared to teach singing and least prepared for improvisation and composition. Orff Schulwerk training was associated with significantly higher confidence in teaching improvisation and composition, whereas participants with Kodály training reported higher levels of confidence for teaching listening. Teachers demonstrated strong confidence for teaching traditional activities (singing, instrument playing) but lower preparedness for creative pedagogy and pedagogical approaches, possibly suggesting gaps in teacher preparation. Responses to open-ended questions revealed participants perceived that their preparation programs emphasized secondary over elementary music education. journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Fundraising Practices of PK–12 Music Teachers in Virginia
abstract: Prior research indicates fundraising is a necessary job function for music educators, yet the how and why of the ways teachers engage in this activity is not well understood. This study sought to investigate the fundraising practices of music educators in the Commonwealth of Virginia. A survey was sent to all members of the Virginia Music Educators Association, as well as solicitations to the fine arts supervisors in the 50 largest districts in the state. Results indicate that teachers raise funds for a variety of expenses, including basic necessities such as instrument repair and required performances. Teachers also reported using many different types of fundraising strategies including item sales, direct appeal (e.g., GoFundMe), and large single events. A majority of teachers agreed with the statements “Fundraising is necessary for me to do my job well” and “I fundraise for materials I believe should be provided through my school budget,” indicating a need for more investigation between school budgets and instructional expectations/teacher evaluation processes. Implications include recommendations for teachers including advocacy talking points.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: The Underlying Mechanisms of Social Bonding in Choral Singing: A Review of the Literature
abstract: Choral singing activates a range of psychological, psychosocial, and physiological mechanisms that shape how participants connect with one another. These mechanisms include interpersonal synchrony, the release of bonding-related neurochemicals, shared heart and respiratory patterns, and psychological processes that support emotional regulation and belonging. The purpose of this literature review is to synthesize interdisciplinary research to explain how these mechanisms interact to enhance social bonding in choral contexts. Integrating group singing into general music classes and applying these principles within choir curricula can support students’ emotional growth, stress management, and peer empathy. By designing activities that emphasize synchrony, coordinated breathing, and collaborative interaction, music educators can intentionally leverage these mechanisms to strengthen classroom communities and foster both social and emotional well-being.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Ensemble Agreements in Popular Music Education: Negotiating Behavior and Collaboration in Student Bands
abstract: This case study investigated how 30 students in a post-secondary popular music diploma program in Singapore co-created and applied ensemble agreements —peer-devised frameworks for guiding rehearsal behavior and communication. Drawing on student-generated documents, reflective questionnaires, and focus group interviews over 1 academic year, the study examined how these agreements influenced collaboration, leadership, accountability, and perceptions of teacher presence. Students initially adopted rule-based, punitive models, but gradually shifted toward dialogic, collaborative approaches emphasizing shared responsibility and mutual respect. Challenges included uneven adherence, blurred responsibility, and negotiating authority between teachers and peers. By year’s end, students viewed ensemble agreements as adaptable frameworks that helped to navigate and maintain professionalism, trust, and collective agency in rehearsal contexts. The findings indicate that ensemble agreements can enhance collaboration and reflective practice in small ensemble settings across varied genres and skill levels.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Active Learning in Music Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Active learning involves instructional approaches that engage students in meaningful thinking and reflection. This work evaluated the effect of active learning on academic achievement in music education. While prior meta-analyses in other disciplines showed positive effects, no quantitative review existed for music. A comprehensive search identified 27 eligible studies, with 20 reporting usable quantitative data. After addressing an outlier, pooled results from 15 independent effect sizes showed a moderate, statistically significant positive effect (ES = 0.46, 95% CI [0.22, 0.70]). Comparisons across groups detected no significant moderation by educational level or strategy, though higher education showed the largest mean effects. Although variation across studies was high, active learning consistently benefited music-specific achievement. The review highlights gaps in methodological rigor and a scarcity of studies in primary and higher education. Overall, findings indicate that active learning enhances achievement in music education, though more high-quality controlled studies are needed.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Belonging: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The authors of the NAfME (National Association for Music Education) Blueprint called for wider K–12 participation, more diverse teacher preparation programs, and reduced professional isolation. Taken together, these priorities center belonging as a core concern for K–12 students, preservice teachers, and inservice educators. This systematic review is a response to the Blueprint by synthesizing the research literature on belonging in music education. A PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)-guided systematic search of major music and education databases yielded 29 articles. Through a thematic analysis of these studies, six themes emerged: (1) cultural identity, (2) peer networks, (3) structural features, (4) pedagogy of care, (5) accessibility, and (6) democratic approaches. Together, these themes show that intentionally inclusive designs can cultivate belonging across ages, abilities, and contexts, whereas competitive ranking or narrow canons of repertoire can erode it. journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Research-to-Resource: Preparing Music Teachers for AI—The AI Literacy Model
abstract: As AI becomes more integrated into our daily lives, AI literacy is emerging as an essential skill. In response to this growing need, the aim of this research-to-resource article is to introduce the AI Literacy Model (AILM) designed to equip preservice music educators. Although AI literacy is increasingly recognized as a crucial skill, its integration into music teacher preparation remains underdeveloped. Building on existing literature, the AILM comprises two dimensions: (a) Core Components of AI literacy: understanding AI, using/applying AI, evaluating AI, and considering AI ethics and (b) the observer-participant-agent pedagogical approach. The first dimension focuses on the core components of AI literacy, detailing what should be taught. To complement this, the second dimension introduces a pedagogical approach grounded in interactive constructivism, emphasizing how to teach these concepts effectively. This article provides both theoretical and practical guidance for cultivating AI literacy in music teacher education.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Research-to-Resource: AI in Music Education Through Heidegger’s Lens: Releasement and Openness to Mystery
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has shifted from a distant prospect to an immediate reality in education, bringing opportunities and challenges. In music education, recent studies emphasize AI’s potential to broaden access, personalize instruction, and foster creativity, while also warning of reduced expressivity, overreliance on automation, and the erosion of human judgment. This duality highlights the need for pedagogical frameworks that balance innovation with critical reflection. Drawing on Heidegger’s insights on technology, this Research-to-Resource article applies the concepts of Releasement ( Gelassenheit ) and Openness to Mystery ( Offenheit für das Geheimnis ) to music education. These concepts invite teachers and students to engage with AI thoughtfully and receptively, viewing its outputs not as finished products but as invitations for interpretation and imaginative exploration. Practical classroom activities illustrate how AI can serve as a reflective and collaborative partner, enriching musical learning while sustaining agency, creativity, and critical judgment.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: “Can You Hear Me Now?”: PK–12 Music Teachers’ Perceptions and Practices Regarding Hearing Health
abstract: In this study, we examined the perceptions and practices of PK–12 music teachers regarding hearing health. Participants ( Ν = 58) completed a questionnaire to assess their use of hearing protection, initiatives to support student hearing health, and perceptions of institutional support for hearing conservation within school settings. Although most teachers reported being aware of noise-related risks and feeling responsible for their hearing health, few consistently wore earplugs or other hearing protection devices. Participants identified several barriers to implementing improved hearing health practices, including physical discomfort with wearing earplugs, access to resources, and support from school administration. Concerns were reported about room acoustics, the long-term effects of noise exposure, and students’ hearing health. Few teachers reported receiving hearing health training from their teacher preparation programs or school districts. This study emphasizes the need for a more comprehensive education, resources, and policy support for hearing health in music education.

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Effects of Expert Modeling During Reciprocal Peer Teaching on Music Performance Outcomes in Fourth Grade String Students
abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the effects of reciprocal peer teaching (RPT) on the music performance skills of fourth grade string students using quasi-experimental, between-subjects designs. Students from a fourth grade orchestra class ( N = 36) were grouped into one of the three conditions: (1) a free interaction RPT group, (2) an identical group, receiving an expert model of interaction strategies prior to RPT, and (3) a control group receiving traditional, whole-class instruction. Students in the experimental groups worked in pairs over six weeks, after which all students completed a performance of French Folk Song for evaluation. Group mean comparisons indicated a significant difference in performance scores between the RPT-only and control groups, with the RPT-only group scoring significantly higher, raising questions regarding the ineffectiveness of the modeling intervention. Results prompt further questions regarding the efficacy of expert modeling during RPT. Music educators, particularly those who work with beginning instrumentalists, are encouraged to implement RPT as an instructional tool to help promote student skill development and pro-social classroom be

journal_name: UPDATE: Applications of Research in Music Education
title: Fostering Autonomous Musical Decision-Making in a Choir of Young Adults With Disabilities: A Case Study
abstract: Individuals with mental disabilities and other adaptive needs may benefit from music education throughout their lives. These individuals are commonly perceived as having decreased autonomy, relatedness, and competence: the three factors contributing to psychological well-being according to self-determination theory (SDT). In this study, we initiated a choral experience with a school for young adults with disabilities. We share findings from conducting autonomy-focused activities embedded in the choral rehearsal. Students and staff in this study share unique outcomes, including the power of decision-making and the importance of leadership and representation.

title: Effects of Planned and Unplanned Ancillary Movements on the Perception of Musical Performance
abstract: Although musicians use movements that are required to produce sound, they also demonstrate expressive movements that are unnecessary for sound production—gestures that are often referred to as “ancillary.” The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of planned and unplanned ancillary movements on observers’ perceptions of musical performances. Participants ( N = 142) were adult community musicians who regularly attended concerts. Participants observed a recording of a trumpet duo performing an etude while demonstrating one of three types of movement (planned ancillary movements, unplanned ancillary movements, and a static condition without ancillary movements). Participants provided ratings of technical accuracy, expressivity, performer communication, and enjoyment. There were no significant main effects for ratings of accuracy or expressivity. However, participants rated performer communication and enjoyment differently based on the type of movements displayed. We offer pedagogical recommendations about ways that music educators can encourage students to use ancillary movements.
